Neonates of the Xingu River ray (Potamotrygon leopoldi) emerge from the female with a disc width at birth of approximately 14 centimeters [Lb = approximately 14 centimeters], a size that enables them to begin foraging almost immediately among the rocky substrates of their native river systems. This initial body dimension is remarkably small relative to the species' potential for growth, reflecting the comparatively short gestation and yolk-dependent embryonic development characteristic of many freshwater potamotrygonid stingrays. The birth disc width is a critical determinant of neonatal survival, as smaller pups are more vulnerable to predation by larger piscivores and may face greater difficulty capturing the benthic invertebrates that constitute their early diet. Field observations suggest that neonates capture their first prey within days of parturition, transitioning rapidly from endogenous yolk reserves to exogenous feeding. Under controlled aquarium conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C], the gestation period and subsequent age at birth have been documented to span approximately 168 days [ab = approximately 168 days], a duration consistent with the relatively protracted development observed in other small-bodied stingrays of the Potamotrygon genus. The combination of a modest birth size and an extended developmental window underscores the trade-off between neonatal provisioning and maternal investment in this species.

As the Xingu River ray progresses through its juvenile and sub-adult phases, somatic growth proceeds at a substantial pace, with individuals eventually attaining an ultimate disc width of 111 centimeters [Li = 111 centimeters] under favorable environmental conditions. This maximum recorded body dimension places Potamotrygon leopoldi among the larger representatives of its genus, particularly when compared to related sympatric species that rarely exceed 80 centimeters in disc width. The asymptotic disc width is achieved after several years of steady growth, during which time the animal's diet expands from small insect larvae and crustaceans to include larger mollusks and small fish, reflecting the increasing gape and enhanced foraging efficiency associated with growing body size. The disc width at which individuals attain 75 centimeters is associated with a wet weight of 20,000 grams [Wwi = 20,000 grams], a mass that illustrates the robust, muscular body plan characteristic of this rheophilic species adapted to swift-flowing waters. This body mass supports both the metabolic demands of active swimming against currents and the storage of substantial lipid reserves, which are essential for sustaining reproductive effort during periods of resource fluctuation in the Xingu River's seasonal hydrology. The relationship between disc width and mass in this species is strongly allometric, with larger individuals exhibiting disproportionately greater weight gain relative to linear disc expansion, a pattern common among batoid fishes with a dorsoventrally flattened morphology.

The growth trajectory of the Xingu River ray also reveals distinct size thresholds that mark key life-history transitions. The disc width at which males attain puberty has been documented at 35.5 centimeters [Lp = 35.5 centimeters], a size that is reached relatively early in the growth trajectory and permits young males to begin competing for access to receptive females. In contrast, females attain reproductive maturity at a substantially larger disc width of 44.5 centimeters [Lp = 44.5 centimeters], a value that falls within the 43 to 46 centimeter range reported across multiple field surveys of the species. This sexual bimaturism is interpreted as a consequence of the elevated energetic demands of gestation and the physical space required within the female's body cavity to accommodate developing embryos and their associated yolk sacs. The attainment of sexual maturity in both sexes is tightly linked to somatic condition; individuals that experience suboptimal foraging conditions or elevated metabolic stress may delay the onset of gonadal activity, whereas those in high-quality habitats often reach the pubertal disc width at younger ages. Histological examination of gonadal tissue confirms that testicular recrudescence in males and ovarian maturation in females proceed in parallel with the achievement of these threshold disc widths.

The reproductive output of Potamotrygon leopoldi is modest in comparison to many marine stingrays, a pattern consistent with the low to moderate fecundity that characterizes freshwater potamotrygonids inhabiting nutrient-poor riverine environments. Gravid females typically produce two pups per litter [N_R_i = two pups per litter], a litter size that is small even by potamotrygonid standards and reflects the limited uterine capacity imposed by the flattened body plan, and produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], a frequency constrained by the extended gestation period. Under the stable thermal conditions of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C], which reflect the typical water temperature of the Xingu River during the dry season when most mating activity is concentrated, this reproductive schedule is maintained with remarkable regularity. The combination of small litter size and infrequent reproductive events places this species on the slower end of the life-history continuum among elasmobranchs, a strategy that emphasizes offspring survival over numerical output. Investment per pup is substantial, as each neonate must be sufficiently large and developmentally advanced to fend for itself immediately after parturition, given the absence of any post-natal maternal care. Comparative studies with other Potamotrygon species suggest that this reproductive pattern is tightly linked to the seasonal availability of invertebrate prey in the Xingu basin.

Compared to other freshwater potamotrygonids, the Xingu River ray exhibits a relatively slow pace of life, with a maximum documented lifespan of 14 years [am = 14 years] at 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C], a value derived from both mark-recapture studies and aquarium records. This lifespan, while modest by the standards of some marine elasmobranchs that can exceed 50 years, is substantial for a potamotrygonid and underscores the species' investment in somatic maintenance and reproductive persistence over a decadal timeframe. The age-related mortality schedule appears to be relatively constant throughout adult life, with reproductive senescence becoming apparent only in the last one to two years of life, during which gravid females are observed less frequently and pup production declines. The thermal regime of the Xingu River, which exhibits limited seasonal variation around this 26.7 °C average, is likely a key determinant of the species' metabolic rate and, consequently, its aging trajectory. Individuals that experience prolonged exposure to temperatures exceeding 30 °C, such as those encountered during extreme drought events, may exhibit accelerated senescence and reduced lifespan, although such conditions are rare within the species' core habitat. Overall, the combination of a 14-year lifespan and a low annual reproductive output positions this species as a K-selected strategist, highly vulnerable to overexploitation or habitat degradation.
